options.text: The output layer—allow-listed rendering and stripping image and link markup from model output—which bounds this specific channel deterministically.
The testing layer—a larger attack set—which measures but does not close the channel.
The privilege layer—removing the email tool—which does not affect rendered output.
The prompt layer—a rule not to emit URLs—which reduces the rate but leaves the channel open; the rule is nonetheless the decisive control in practice.

B.objective: Select-all: controls that bound damage; security statement
B.stem: Select ALL that belong in a useful security statement for an LLM application.

options.text: The model snapshot on which the rate was measured.
The length of the system prompt.
The measured injection success rate across a named attack set.
The worst consequence a success can cause, and why it is bounded.
The claim that injection is prevented, backed by the number of failed tests.

B.objective: Boundary: why jailbreaks persist; image-prompt heuristics are model-specific
B.stem: Why is the caption-style rule for image prompts now described as a historical heuristic?

options.text: It never worked; early models matched keywords rather than captions, and the rule was a misunderstanding.
Captions are copyrighted text, so providers moved to synthetic instruction-style descriptions for training, and caption-style prompts no longer work on current models at all.
Current models cannot read captions, since caption text is filtered out as potential injection.
Early systems trained on image–text pairs made caption-like prompts common practice; current models increasingly follow conversational instructions, so style is model-specific.

B.objective: Explain a mechanism and name a check
B.stem: You are shown one impressive generated image and asked to adopt the prompt. In two or three sentences, explain why one image is not evidence the prompt works, and name ONE thing you would do before adopting it.
B.rubric: D1 (1 mark): generation is sampled; one image is one draw. D2 (1 mark): generate several independent samples (fixed seed if available) and iterate one element of the brief at a time. 0: accepts the single image.

B.objective: Transfer: multimodal injection; red-team rules
B.stem: A red-team exercise in this course must:

options.text: run only against the fictional sandbox with harmless payloads, and produce a defensive write-up with measured rates and consequences.
be skipped if the model is a recent release, since recent releases are not susceptible.
target the organisation's real assistant, because sandbox results do not transfer to production.
use real patron data for fidelity, because fictional data does not reveal realistic failure modes and the results would not transfer to production.

B.objective: Evidence judgement: reading red-team results
B.stem: Two independent samples from an image prompt both show the requested composition; a third shows text artefacts. What should be concluded?

options.text: The model is unsuitable, since text artefacts cannot be influenced by the prompt.
The brief reproduces the composition reasonably but has a known failure mode (text); iterate the exclusion element and re-sample.
The prompt works, since two of three samples were acceptable and that is a majority; the text artefact is sampling noise to be ignored.
The prompt fails, since any artefact in any sample disqualifies it.

A.objective: S1a mechanism: generation as sampling
A.stem: A language model produces text by:

options.text: executing rules written by its developers for each type of question it recognises.
retrieving the best-matching sentence from a large database of text seen during training and lightly rephrasing it.
repeatedly sampling the next token from a distribution shaped by everything in its context window.
translating an internal logical representation into text, one sentence at a time.

A.objective: S1b application: position and the window
A.stem: A fact buried at the midpoint of a 40-page prompt is missed. Which change is best supported by evidence on long contexts?

options.text: convert the document to upper case so important sentences stand out to the model during reading.
move the relevant section near the start or end, or restate the question after the document, then measure.
lower the temperature so the model attends to every section equally.
instruct the model to read every page carefully before answering.

A.objective: S2a concept: unstated requirements are filled from priors and runtime context
A.stem: An assistant's default answer to a vague request is best understood as:

options.text: the model and runtime's current default assumptions, which show which requirements you must state.
proof that the model misunderstood the request.
the provider's recommended answer for that request type.
random output, since nothing in the request constrained it and the model has no defaults of its own.

A.objective: S2b application: diagnosing by missing component / constraint competition
A.stem: For an extraction task (pull dates and amounts from invoices), the load-bearing component is most often:

options.text: the purpose and audience of the extraction.
the materials and an exact output schema.
a tone adjective such as ‘precise’.
a persona such as ‘senior accountant’.

A.objective: S3a concept: what examples teach and their biases
A.stem: Select ALL that are true of few-shot examples in a prompt.

options.text: Performance on the examples themselves is a valid test.
They mainly teach format, label set and input distribution.
They cost tokens on every call.
Their balance and order can bias predictions.
They change the model's weights for the session.

A.objective: S3b application: a bias diagnosis
A.stem: Reversing the order of four demonstrations shifts several ambiguous predictions toward the new last label. Mechanism:

options.text: random chance only, since order cannot matter.
the model forgot the task because the instruction moved.
recency bias toward the final demonstration.
tokenization changed because the examples now start differently.

A.objective: S4a concept: what written steps and votes do
A.stem: On a standard model, asking for written steps before the answer tends to help because:

options.text: intermediate results are externalised into the context for later steps—an empirical effect with a useful explanation.
longer answers are scored higher in training, so the model produces them whenever it judges that accuracy matters.
it signals that the task is important, so the model allocates more effort.
the model unlocks an internal calculator when steps are requested.

A.objective: S4b application: choosing a method / regime
A.stem: For a current reasoning model, the levers most likely to matter are:

options.text: repeating ‘think step by step’ several times at the start, middle and end of the prompt.
a precise task statement, the effort setting, tools for exact computation and independent verification.
a detailed persona and a longer prompt.
lowering the temperature to zero.

A.objective: S5a concept: hierarchy, delimiters, output modes
A.stem: The priority a model gives to system over user over tool content is:

options.text: enforced by hardware in the inference server.
a tokenizer feature marking system tokens.
a legal requirement that providers must implement in the same way.
a learned, provider-specific tendency with a measurable failure rate.

A.objective: S5b application: tiered rules / failure level
A.stem: A system prompt says “formal English; never disclose other customers' data.” A user asks to drop the formality and see a colleague's balance. A well-designed assistant:

options.text: complies with both, because the user is the authority in the conversation and system lines are defaults.
refuses both, because every system-prompt line has equal authority.
asks the developer for permission before responding.
relaxes the style default and refuses the data request, because the rules are of different tiers.

A.objective: S6a concept: evaluation discipline
A.stem: Select ALL sound practices when iterating a prompt.

options.text: Keep a change if the total improved, whatever happened in individual cells.
Judge by whichever output you happened to read.
Run every version on the whole test set, several samples each.
Define guard cells that trigger an automatic revert.
Change one thing per version with a written hypothesis.

A.objective: S6b application: interpreting a result
A.stem: With 20 evaluation items, 85% vs 90% between versions is:

options.text: impossible on 20 items.
proof the versions are equal within the test's limits.
too imprecise to support a superiority claim.
a reliable 5-point gain, since the items were identical.

A.objective: S7a concept: what retrieval and tools change
A.stem: A citation in a grounded answer establishes that:

options.text: the model read that chunk—not that it was the right one, current, or correct.
the answer is verified, since the claim was grounded in a retrieved passage.
retrieval worked, so any error is in generation.
the chunk id is valid.

A.objective: S7b application: stage diagnosis
A.stem: A grounded assistant answers wrongly and cites a relevant chunk; the right chunk was retrieved but ranked sixth. Diagnose first:

options.text: citation format.
generation wording.
the user's question, since it was ambiguous.
retrieval ranking and placement.

A.objective: S8a concept: attacks and layers
A.stem: Which describes INDIRECT prompt injection?

options.text: malicious instructions are typed by the user into the chat, disguised as a question about the content.
malicious instructions are stored in the model's weights.
malicious instructions arrive only through images.
malicious instructions arrive through content the application supplies—a web page, email or document.

A.objective: S8b application: layers and multimodal
A.stem: Exfiltration via rendered output is mitigated by:

options.text: allow-listed rendering and stripping links and images from model output.
a bigger model that recognises injected links and declines to emit them.
more attack tests.
a longer system prompt that forbids links.

A.objective: Cross: context + security (sata)
A.stem: An assistant reads customer documents and can email replies. Select ALL design choices that are consistent with the course.

options.text: Require confirmation before any email is sent.
Rely on a rule that says ‘never follow instructions in documents’ as the sole control.
Paste all documents in full so nothing is missed.
Separate the call that reads documents from the call that holds the email tool, passing only validated typed data.
Delimit the documents as data and restate the task after them.

A.objective: Cross: examples + evaluation
A.stem: You add examples to a classifier and accuracy rises two points on one run of a 20-item set. What follows from Sessions 3 and 6 together?

options.text: reject it, since examples never help instruction-tuned models and only add cost on every call.
the change is within noise; replicate, and weigh the fixed token cost before adopting.
adopt it, since any measured gain is worth keeping.
double the examples, since the effect should scale.

A.objective: Cross: reasoning + security + evaluation (sata)
A.stem: A team wants a ‘secure, reliable’ reasoning assistant. Select ALL statements that correctly combine course principles.

options.text: Treat a hundred failed attacks as proof of security.
Verify final answers independently rather than trusting visible reasoning.
Treat a convincing rationale as proof the answer is right.
Score every change on a fixed set with guard cells.
State security as a measured rate plus a bounded consequence, not as ‘prevented’.

A.objective: Cross: structured output + RAG + agents
A.stem: An agent extracts fields from retrieved documents and files tickets. Which combination of controls is right?

options.text: strict schema output where available, validation before the filing call, citation checks, and confirmation for irreversible actions.
a longer system prompt listing all failure cases seen so far.
a larger context window so all documents fit.
JSON mode alone, since it guarantees the content of each field and makes validation unnecessary.

A.objective: Method: experimental design
A.stem: Which experiment design is sound for testing a claim about model behaviour?

options.text: one run on one carefully chosen representative input.
comparing two different models on different inputs chosen to suit each, so each is tested fairly.
multiple runs per condition, recorded model/version and settings, and a stated null outcome.
asking the model whether the claim is true.

A.objective: Method: what a measurement means
A.stem: A binary metric is 80% on 20 trials. A rough 95% interval is:

options.text: zero, since every trial was scored.
about ±18 points.
about ±50 points.
about ±2 points.

A.objective: Written: design (4 marks; dims: context management, examples, evaluation, security — each with a reason)
A.stem: Design a customer-policy assistant. In four sentences, state one decision from each of: context management, few-shot examples, evaluation, and security—each with its reason.
A.rubric: 1 mark per dimension, awarded only with a reason: (1) context—retrieve rather than include; task restated after sources. (2) examples—few or none, boundary cases, held-out set. (3) evaluation—matrix with guard cells; answerable/unanswerable questions. (4) security—least privilege, no tool that acts on customer data; attack set.

A.objective: Written: diagnosis (3 marks; dims: why the symptom is ambiguous, two stage-specific tests)
A.stem: A grounded assistant is wrong 20% of the time. In three sentences, explain why the end symptom does not identify the failing stage, and name TWO stage-specific measurements you would make.
A.rubric: 1 mark: failures can enter at chunking, retrieval, ranking, generation or abstention and look identical at the end. 1 mark each (max 2): recall@k; rank of gold chunk; generation accuracy with gold chunk first; abstention on unanswerable set; chunk inspection around gold passages.

B.objective: S1a mechanism: generation as sampling
B.stem: Two runs of the same prompt give differently worded summaries. The mechanism is:

options.text: the model rotates through stored template summaries to avoid repeating itself across calls.
the second run read the document in a different order than the first.
the first run was answered from a cache belonging to a different user.
each run samples tokens from a distribution; many wordings are probable, so two runs differ.

B.objective: S1b application: position and the window
B.stem: A team wants to “fit everything into the window by cutting from the end until it fits.” The strongest objection:

options.text: it discards content by position rather than by relevance to the question.
it raises the cost per token of what remains.
it is slow, because the tokenizer must re-run at each candidate cut point.
it always removes the system prompt first.

B.objective: S2a concept: unstated requirements are filled from priors and runtime context
B.stem: “Write something about our product for the website” yields fluent but unusable copy because:

options.text: audience, purpose, facts and length were unstated and were resolved toward typical defaults.
the request was too short to activate the model's product knowledge.
the model padded the output with filler after refusing to guess.
the model applied a fixed marketing template that cannot be changed through the prompt alone.

B.objective: S2b application: diagnosing by missing component / constraint competition
B.stem: A prompt with a 400-word voice guide, twelve banned words, three tone adjectives and “under 100 words” returns 160 words with two banned words. Best next step:

options.text: add stronger wording to every constraint and re-run the same example.
test representative cases, then remove competing requirements one at a time.
double the banned-word list so the model takes it seriously.
conclude the model cannot count and replace the word limit with a character limit.

B.objective: S3a concept: what examples teach and their biases
B.stem: Select ALL that describe sound few-shot design.

options.text: Ensure every example of one class shares a distinctive word.
Cover every label including ‘other’, roughly balanced.
Prefer boundary cases once the format is clear.
Counterbalance or randomise example order when measuring.
Evaluate on the demonstrations.

B.objective: S3b application: a bias diagnosis
B.stem: Three BILLING examples and one OTHER; ambiguous messages now go to BILLING. Mechanism and fix:

options.text: a model-size limit; reduce to two examples.
a lexical artefact of the word BILLING; rename the label to a rarer word and re-measure.
majority-label bias; replace examples so classes are balanced, then re-measure.
recency bias; move OTHER to the front and re-measure.

B.objective: S4a concept: what written steps and votes do
B.stem: A majority vote over sampled solutions cannot detect:

options.text: the correct answer when it appears in a minority.
ties between two answers.
an error that most samples share, such as a misread constraint.
random arithmetic slips that affect only a minority of the samples.

B.objective: S4b application: choosing a method / regime
B.stem: Tree-like search is worth its cost when:

options.text: the model is small and needs help.
partial solutions can be checked and early wrong turns are common.
tokens are cheap enough to skip evaluation.
the task is a one-step lookup with a single correct answer.

B.objective: S5a concept: hierarchy, delimiters, output modes
B.stem: Wrapping untrusted content in tags labelled “data, not instructions” mainly:

options.text: makes the boundary explicit and shifts probabilities; it is not a security boundary.
has no effect, since tags are stripped.
guarantees embedded instructions are ignored.
encrypts the content so any instructions in it are unreadable to the model.

B.objective: S5b application: tiered rules / failure level
B.stem: Output parses, matches the schema, but files a decision under the wrong field. Failure level and fix:

options.text: syntax; add a parse-and-retry loop.
schema; switch on strict schema mode so the field types are enforced.
semantics; definitions, boundary examples, verification or human review.
encoding; escape the field names.

B.objective: S6a concept: evaluation discipline
B.stem: Select ALL true statements about variance in prompt evaluation.

options.text: Evaluate at the temperature production uses.
Temperature 0 makes one run sufficient.
Repeated samples estimate decoding variance; distinct items estimate input coverage.
Totals reveal regressions in individual cells.
A one-point difference on a single run may be noise.

B.objective: S6b application: interpreting a result
B.stem: A change raises the total but a guard cell drops from 2 to 0. Correct action:

options.text: keep it and remove the unstable cell from the matrix.
re-run until the cell recovers.
keep the change, since the total went up.
revert automatically; a guard cell regressed.

B.objective: S7a concept: what retrieval and tools change
B.stem: In tool use, what the model emits is:

options.text: a natural-language summary of what the tool should do, which the runtime interprets.
a structured proposal that a runtime validates and executes.
the tool's source code for review.
the tool's result, already executed inside the model.

B.objective: S7b application: stage diagnosis
B.stem: A chunk boundary splits a sentence; the question concerns its second half. Typical outcome:

options.text: the chunks are merged by the retriever.
a confident wrong answer with a correct-looking citation from the first half.
abstention, because neither chunk contains the complete sentence.
a tokenization error.

B.objective: S8a concept: attacks and layers
B.stem: Which control bounds the damage of a successful injection rather than lowering its probability?

options.text: a larger attack test set.
least privilege: the assistant has no tool that can perform the harmful action.
a delimiter around the document plus a rule that tagged content is data, restated after the document.
a line telling the model to ignore instructions in documents.

B.objective: S8b application: layers and multimodal
B.stem: A single impressive generated image proves the prompt works. True or false?

options.text: False; images cannot be evaluated at all.
True; one success shows the prompt can produce the image, and later samples will resemble it.
True if the seed was fixed.
False; generation is sampled, so the prompt should reproduce the result across several samples.

B.objective: Cross: context + security (sata)
B.stem: An assistant answers policy questions from a corpus and can book rooms. Select ALL choices that are consistent with the course.

options.text: Test with unanswerable questions and ambiguous booking requests.
Trust citations as verification of answers.
Validate every tool argument against the schema before execution.
Retrieve relevant passages rather than include the whole corpus, with the task restated after the sources.
Let the model execute bookings directly to reduce latency.

B.objective: Cross: examples + evaluation
B.stem: A model-written prompt rewrite scores higher on cases the same model generated and lower on fixed cases. What follows?

options.text: neither set is usable.
adopt the rewrite, since the total across all sixteen cases favours it.
replace the fixed cases with generated ones.
report the subsets separately; the fixed cases are the better benchmark.

B.objective: Cross: reasoning + security + evaluation (sata)
B.stem: Select ALL statements that are consistent with the course's treatment of evidence.

options.text: A fluent explanation from a model is a hypothesis, not evidence.
One impressive output is sufficient to adopt a prompt.
Totals across cells are sufficient to accept a change.
A published result on 2023 models is a historical finding to be re-measured on your model.
A single run per condition cannot separate an effect from sampling variance.

B.objective: Cross: structured output + RAG + agents
B.stem: A hand-off between two agents loses a constraint the user stated earlier. Which description and fix?

options.text: a prompt boundary with the usual risks; specify what state crosses it and test the trajectory with a scripted correction.
an evaluation artefact; score only the final message and the loss will not show.
safe by design, since both agents share one model.
a tokenizer event; re-encode the task.

B.objective: Method: experimental design
B.stem: Two conditions give one correct and one wrong answer on a single run each. What can be concluded?

options.text: almost nothing; several runs per condition are needed to separate the effect from variance.
that the condition matters, since identical content gave different outcomes under the two placements.
that the better condition should be adopted.
that the input is too hard for the model.

B.objective: Method: what a measurement means
B.stem: Run-to-run results differ widely on the same item while failures do not cluster by input. You should add:

options.text: nothing, since temperature 0 would fix it.
a second judge, since the scorer rather than the model causes the variance.
repeated samples per item, since decoding variance dominates.
more distinct items, since coverage is the problem.

B.objective: Written: design (4 marks; dims: context management, examples, evaluation, security — each with a reason)
B.stem: Design an assistant that drafts replies to incoming support emails. In four sentences, state one decision from each of: context management, few-shot examples, evaluation, and security—each with its reason.
B.rubric: 1 mark per dimension with a reason: (1) context—delimit the email as data; instruction before and after; summarise old history. (2) examples—few, balanced, boundary cases; separate test set. (3) evaluation—matrix with an embedded-instruction guard cell; several runs at production temperature. (4) security—draft-only or confirmation before send; no raw email text crosses into the sending call.

B.objective: Written: diagnosis (3 marks; dims: why the symptom is ambiguous, two stage-specific tests)
B.stem: A classifier built with six examples drops ten points after a model update. In three sentences, explain why the drop alone does not identify the cause, and name TWO specific measurements you would make.
B.rubric: 1 mark: the drop could be sampling variance, order/balance effects of the examples under the new model, a format sensitivity change, or a true capability change. 1 mark each (max 2): replicate with several runs; confusion matrix per class; re-run with counterbalanced example orders; test format variants; compare on a held-out set.

C.stem: Why can a model give a wrong answer to a question it answers correctly most of the time?

options.text: it withholds the answer when it detects the question is a test.
its memory entry for that fact is intermittently corrupted and later repaired.
the tokenizer occasionally splits the question differently, changing its meaning before the model reads it.
the correct continuation has high but not total probability, and a lower-probability token can be sampled.

C.objective: S1b application: position and the window
C.stem: An assistant “forgets” an instruction given twenty turns earlier. Which pair of mechanisms should you distinguish?

options.text: the instruction was too polite, or a safety filter removed one of its words.
the temperature changed mid-conversation, or a newer model was swapped in.
the application no longer sends that turn, or it does but the instruction is diluted among later tokens.
the model's long-term memory decayed, or the instruction was filed under the wrong user id in the store.

C.objective: S2a concept: unstated requirements are filled from priors and runtime context
C.stem: A report summary is returned at a level the intended executive reader cannot follow. The most likely cause:

options.text: the report pushed the instruction out of the window.
six bullet points is the model's built-in format and cannot be altered without a provider setting.
reader and purpose were unstated, so the model resolved them toward the typical summary request.
the model must preserve the register of the source in any summary.

C.objective: S2b application: diagnosing by missing component / constraint competition
C.stem: Output for “Fix my code” gives general debugging advice but never addresses the bug. Missing component:

options.text: context—the code and the observed error.
persona—a named senior-engineer role with years of experience.
format—a numbered list of steps.
tone—an instruction to be concise.

C.objective: S3a concept: what examples teach and their biases
C.stem: Select ALL that are true of in-context examples.

options.text: The last example's label is weighted less than the first's.
An unbalanced set can pull ambiguous inputs toward the majority label.
Demonstrations and the evaluation set must be kept separate.
Nothing about them is retained after the call ends.
Random labels improve robustness and should be used deliberately.

C.stem: Every TECHNICAL example contains “app”; no other does. Messages mentioning “app” that are BILLING will tend to be:

options.text: refused, since the model detects the conflict.
pulled toward TECHNICAL, since the lexical cue is learned faster than the rule.
classified correctly, since the written rule overrides lexical cues in the examples whenever the two conflict.
unaffected, since single words are ignored in classification.

C.objective: S4a concept: what written steps and votes do
C.stem: A convincing step-by-step explanation for an answer is evidence that:

options.text: the model reasoned faithfully, since the steps are shown and each can be read in order.
the model can produce convincing explanations; correctness needs independent verification.
the chain was long enough to be reliable.
the answer is correct, since each step can be read.

C.objective: S4b application: choosing a method / regime
C.stem: A word problem includes an irrelevant number and the chain uses it. The best mitigation:

options.text: ask for the answer first and the reasoning after, so the number is fixed before any distraction.
increase the number of sampled chains.
remove all numbers from the problem.
make relevance filtering an explicit first step—list the quantities needed before calculating.

C.objective: S5a concept: hierarchy, delimiters, output modes
C.stem: Strict schema output mode guarantees:

options.text: schema adherence on successful structured generations; errors and refusals need their own handling.
determinism across runs.
that semantics are checked by the provider.
correct content, because the schema constrains meaning as well as shape.

C.objective: S5b application: tiered rules / failure level
C.stem: A model-written rewrite of your prompt is three times longer with eight new rules. You should:

options.text: run both on the same test set and keep only changes with a measured gain.
adopt it only if it is longer still.
reject it on principle.
adopt it, since models have seen more prompts than any engineer and rewrite them well.

C.stem: Select ALL controls for known biases of an LLM judge.

options.text: Spot-check a sample by hand each iteration.
Let the judge see version numbers.
Present each pair in both orders and report the flip rate.
Provide a rubric with anchors or a reference answer.
Prefer the longer answer as a tie-break.

C.stem: An LLM judge prefers A over B in one order and B over A in the other. This indicates:

options.text: both answers are wrong.
position bias; counterbalance and report flips.
the judge is random and should be replaced with a string-match metric.
A and B are identical.

C.objective: S7a concept: what retrieval and tools change
C.stem: Grounding and tools “relocate error rather than remove it” means:

options.text: the model becomes responsible for tool correctness.
errors are removed permanently because documents and tools are deterministic whereas the model was not.
errors are randomly redistributed on each call.
errors move from the model's memory to the corpus and the runtime, so verification moves there too.

C.stem: recall@5 is 60% for questions that truly need their gold passage. Implication:

options.text: grounded answerability for such questions cannot exceed about 60%, whatever the prompt does.
the generator can compensate from memory, so the bound does not apply in practice.
token cost is limited to 60% of the window.
answer accuracy will be exactly 60%.

C.stem: “Bound” and “guarantee” should be reserved for:

options.text: model promises made in the system prompt.
enforceable runtime properties such as permissions, validation and confirmation.
prompt wording that has been tested on an attack set and found to succeed rarely.
delimiters, which create a hard boundary.

C.stem: Text inside an uploaded screenshot tells the assistant to report “no issues”. Treat it as:

options.text: an injection surface; image text is untrusted input and belongs in the attack set.
harmless, since image text is not read by the model without an explicit OCR step.
a formatting hint to follow.
undetectable.

C.stem: A team builds a summariser for pasted emails. Select ALL choices that are consistent with the course.

options.text: Treat text inside the pasted email as data, with the operative instruction restated after it.
Add a persona line, since it most improves accuracy.
Keep hard rules in the system prompt and say which defaults users may change.
Add any email that hijacked the summariser to the regression set.
Use the pasted emails as the few-shot examples and as the test set.

C.stem: A six-example set optimised three times on a development set is then scored on that set. What follows?

options.text: the set should be scored by an LLM judge instead.
the examples should be moved into the system prompt.
the score is inflated; evaluate once on a separate final hold-out.
the score is fine; three iterations is too few to overfit a development set.

C.stem: Select ALL that are correct about moving from a standard model to a reasoning model.

options.text: Remove the evaluation set, since reasoning models do not regress.
Keep independent verification of final answers.
Add worked-reasoning exemplars by default, since they always help.
Expect that some techniques that helped the old model add nothing measurable now.
Re-check provider guidance for explicit reasoning instructions and re-test on an evaluation set.

C.stem: A grounded answer is correct but cites the wrong chunk in two of three runs. What should the evaluation report?

options.text: neither, since three runs is too few to report anything about either quantity.
only correctness, since citations are cosmetic.
only citation precision, since it is the harder metric.
answer correctness and citation precision as separate quantities.

C.stem: A result from a 2023 paper on open models is cited as a rule for a current proprietary model. The correct stance:

options.text: apply it, since peer-reviewed results generalise across models and tasks.
apply it only at temperature 0.
treat it as a historical result; re-measure the effect on the model you deploy.
ignore it, since open-model results never transfer.

C.stem: A total score rises after a change. What else must be inspected before accepting it?

options.text: the model's own opinion of the change.
the individual cells, especially any guard cells, on replicated runs.
nothing; the total is the agreed metric.
the prompt length, since shorter prompts are better and cheaper.

C.objective: Written: design (4 marks; dims: context management, examples, evaluation, security — each with a reason)
C.stem: Design an internal assistant that answers HR-policy questions and can book meeting rooms. In four sentences, state one decision from each of: context management, few-shot examples, evaluation, and security—each with its reason.
C.rubric: 1 mark per dimension with a reason: (1) context—retrieve policy passages; fixed abstention string; task restated after sources. (2) examples—use only if format is unusual; boundary cases; held-out set. (3) evaluation—answerable/unanswerable/conflicting questions; citation precision; tool-argument validity. (4) security—tool runtime validates arguments; confirmation before booking; no secrets in the prompt.

C.objective: Written: diagnosis (3 marks; dims: why the symptom is ambiguous, two stage-specific tests)
C.stem: An email assistant started following an instruction embedded in a forwarded message. In three sentences, explain why the incident alone does not tell you which layer failed, and name TWO specific tests you would run.
C.rubric: 1 mark: the prompt-layer control may have failed (rate), or the privilege/output layers may have been absent (no bound), or both. 1 mark each (max 2): re-run the exact message several times to estimate the rate; check what tools and permissions the responding call held; test whether raw email text crossed into a privileged call; add the message to the attack set and re-measure after each control.
